items.item: moto's local S3-compatible server reproduces the HTTP-level protocol contract (conditional headers, 412 responses, ETags) faithfully, but its consistency and latency are an in-memory simulation, not a measurement of real AWS network behavior — this topic's demo verifies the protocol, not the production performance characteristics.

The 'no atomic rename' demonstration stops deliberately between copy_object and delete_object to show a reachable crash state; in normal, uninterrupted operation the rename completes both calls and the old key is removed, so this isn't a claim that renames routinely leave duplicates, only that nothing in the protocol prevents it when something goes wrong between the two calls.

at.step: Reveal: no atomic rename, demonstrated for real

items.item: The LIST-cost measurement asserts round-trip count (5 calls for 250 objects at 50 per page), not wall-clock latency, specifically because local-loopback timing in this sandbox isn't representative of real S3 network latency — the call-count scaling is the real, deterministic fact being demonstrated.

at.step: Reveal: LIST isn't free

items.item: If-None-Match and If-Match solve different problems: If-None-Match is for creating a key that must not already exist (a new commit), while If-Match is for updating a key whose current state you've already read (a compare-and-swap) — conflating them would silently accept a creation that should have failed, or reject a legitimate first write.

at.step: Reveal: If-Match is the same primitive for updates

items.item: Strong read-after-write consistency and the atomicity of a single PUT are two different guarantees — S3 has always made a single object's write atomic (you never see a partially-written object), but before December 2020 the visibility of a successful write to a subsequent read could still be delayed, which is the specific guarantee the Dec 2020 change added.

at.step: Reveal: strong consistency, since December 2020

items.item: GCS and ADLS are cited here as the two other major providers with their own strongly-consistent read/write guarantees, not because their conditional-write mechanics are identical to S3's — ADLS, for instance, supports ETag-based conditional headers including a wildcard for 'only if absent,' the same shape as S3's but through Azure's own REST API, not a literal port of S3's headers.

Request pricing is named in this topic's own outcomes as a real cost category every later table-format topic has to budget for, but this topic does not quantify a dollar figure for it — it is disclosed as unquantified in post-notes.md's Frontier section rather than silently omitted.

Per-prefix request-rate limits (at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE or 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second) apply per partitioned prefix, not per bucket — a bucket with many prefixes has no overall limit on the number of prefixes, so the real mitigation for a hot workload is spreading writes across more prefixes, not treating the whole bucket as rate-limited.

at.step: Reveal: LIST isn't free

items.item: The December 2020 change made strong consistency the automatic default for every S3 customer with no opt-in and no application changes required — it wasn't a new API or a new header, just a change in the guarantee behind the same existing requests.

at.step: Reveal: strong consistency, since December 2020

items.item: This topic's own handoff names the specific failure this substrate's limits caused historically: Hive's plain directory-as-partition tables, which depended on exactly the atomic-rename and fast-listing guarantees object storage doesn't provide — the next topic picks that failure up directly.
